item.title: [JAMA] Review of Management of Long-Term Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease
item.description: To the Editor A recent Review provided a comprehensive discussion regarding long-term management of patients born with cyanotic congenital heart disease. As maternal-fetal medicine specialists, we would like to highlight the maternal and neonatal risks associated with both repaired and unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease in pregnancy and emphasize that all of these reproductive-aged patients should have pregnancy intentions routinely evaluated and be provided access to contraception, preconception, and multidisciplinary pregnancy care as appropriate.

item.title: [JAMA] Review of Adult Male Hypogonadism
item.description: To the Editor A recent Review of adult male hypogonadism thoroughly discussed several important treatment-related adverse effects and safety considerations of testosterone use, including erythrocytosis, venous thromboembolic events, blood pressure elevation, and prostate-related monitoring. However, one clinically important adverse effect of testosterone therapy was overlooked: suppression of spermatogenesis and the subsequent risk of infertility in reproductive-aged men.

item.title: [JAMA] Review of Management of Long-Term Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease—In Reply
item.description: In Reply We thank Dr Jones and colleagues for their thoughtful comments regarding our Review on survivors of cyanotic congenital heart disease and for highlighting the critical importance of reproductive health in women with congenital heart disease. We fully agree that reproductive counseling should be an integral component of lifelong care, particularly for women with complex congenital heart disease, and appreciate the opportunity to further emphasize this important aspect.

item.title: [JAMA] Review of Adult Male Hypogonadism—Reply

item.description: One critical shortcoming of many clinical therapeutic trials is their focus on short-term effects, leaving unanswered questions about how participants fare in the longer term. Trial extension studies are conducted to address this gap, allowing assessment of both durability of treatment benefit (eg, whether disease remission or improvements in function are maintained or diminished over time) and long-term safety (such as incidence of delayed adverse events). item.description: If medicine too readily imagines the body as machine, the poem “Eternal life” proposes poetry itself as a deeper, more marvelously humane technology. Against a searchable database and a website’s archived obituary photographs, the poem offers its own elegant processing, synthesis, and preservation, which do not merely confirm whether someone has died, but restore the departed in the small gestures that make each one memorably human. item.description: To the Editor I read with great interest the TRACK trial and the insightful accompanying Editorial regarding the use of low-dose rivaroxaban in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD). Although the investigators should be commended for undertaking this trial in a historically excluded population, the lack of cardiovascular efficacy and significant increase in major bleeding events highlight critical methodological limitations that warrant a strategic paradigm shift in future trial designs involving direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) in end-stage kidney disease.

We agree with Dr Coppi that the results of our trial demonstrated that much of the cardiovascular disease in advanced kidney disease may not be atherothrombotic in nature and therefore may not be modifiable by atherothrombotic treatments. item.title: [JAMA] Understanding Patent Thickets
item.description: Prescription drug manufacturers typically apply to the US Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for patents to protect their products from generic competition. The primary patent on a drug covers the core active ingredient and generally lasts 20 years. Because these patents are often granted early in drug development, however, the effective period of patent protection after US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval is usually 7 to 12 years. item.title: [JAMA] Azithromycin for Cesarean Delivery
item.description: Preventing maternal morbidity and mortality remains an urgent global priority, yet progress has been unsatisfactory. Although maternal mortality has declined globally, the rates have increased in the US and infections are among the top causes of preventable deaths. Among women undergoing cesarean delivery (the most common major surgical procedure in the US), the risk of infection is many times higher than after vaginal delivery, underscoring the importance of effective prophylaxis.

item.title: [JAMA] Small Gains but Persistent Gaps in Statin Adherence
item.description: Few problems in cardiovascular medicine have proved as resistant as adherence to effective medications. Nonadherence is pervasive and arises from the interplay of patient, treatment, clinician, payer, and health system factors. Decades of interventions to improve medication adherence have addressed forgetfulness, education, treatment complexity, and out-of-pocket costs, but have produced inconsistent or incremental gains, underscoring that nonadherence does not have a single remedy.
